Long afterwards, in 1880, Adams was again in London when Lowell came as Minister; and he had Bright to dinner. Bright was then in the Cabinet, but still rare in society. At the end, over the wine, he took possession of the table in his old way, and ended with a denunciation of the Bench, spoken in his massive manner, as though every word were a hammer:—

"For two hundred years, the Judges of England sat on the Bench, condemning to the penalty of death every man, woman, and child who stole property to the value of five shillings; and, during all that time, not one Judge ever remonstrated against the law. We English are a nation of brutes, and ought to be exterminated to the last man."

As they rose from table, Adams said to Lowell that Bright was very fine. "Yes!" replied Lowell, "but too violent!"

Precisely this was the point Adams doubted. Bright knew what violence of language was necessary to drive an idea into a Lancashire head; he kept his own head cool. What shocked Lowell was that he denounced his own people. Yet Bright was personally disliked by his victims, but not distrusted; they never doubted what he would do next, as they did with Russell, Gladstone, and Disraeli. He betrayed no one, and never advanced an opinion in practical matters which did not prove to be practical.

The class who set themselves up as Bright's intellectual opposites — the trimmers, the political economists, the doctrinaires, the followers of de Tocqueville and of John Stuart Mill — seemed the weakest and most eccentric of all. They were timid, with good reason; and timidity, which is high wisdom in philosophy, sicklies the whole cast of thought in action. Like the anti-slavery doctrinaires of the forties and fifties, they became mute and useless when slavery struck them in the face. Their attitude of oscillating reserve seemed to an American more eccentric than the reckless hostility of Brougham or Carlyle, and more mischievous, for he never could be sure what preposterous commonplace it might encourage.

The sum of these experiences in 1863 left the conviction that eccentricity was weakness. The young American who should adopt English thought was lost. The years of Palmerston's last Cabinet, 1859 to 1865, were avowedly years of truce — of arrested development. The British system, like the French, was in its last stage of decomposition. Never had the British mind shown itself so *décousu* — so unravelled, at sea, floundering in every sort of historical shipwreck. A young American in 1863 could see little or nothing of the future. He might dream, but he could not foretell, the suddenness with which the old Europe, with England in its wake, was to vanish in 1870. He was in dead-water, and the parti-colored, fantastic cranks swam about his boat, as though he were the ancient mariner, and they saurians of the prime.
